lessons.title: Lesson 1: How AI is used in music, and the ground rules
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain three ways AI is used in music and the rules you will follow.
This lesson builds toward: Thinking about music you hear and make, you will explain how AI is used in music and the ground rules you will follow, naming three uses and the rules on copying, voices, age limits and honesty.
AI is used in music in many ways: apps that suggest chords or drum patterns, tools that clean up recordings, assistants like ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini that help brainstorm lyrics, and generators that create whole songs from a text prompt.
In this course, AI is your brainstorming partner. You make the main creative choices. That matters for learning, and it matters legally too: the U.S. Copyright Office has said that typing prompts alone is not enough to make you the author of what an AI produces. Your own words, sounds and arrangement are what count.
Ground rules: do not copy other people's songs, do not use an AI copy of a real singer's or classmate's voice, check the age rules of each tool, follow your school's AI rules for music class, and be honest about how you used AI.
Words to know:
- AI music generator: a tool that creates music from a text description.
- Author: the person who creates a work and can own its copyright.
- Prompt: what you type to ask an AI for something.
Official sources:
- U.S. Copyright Office: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2 (copyrightability)
- U.S. Copyright Office: Copyright and AI
Try it now: Write the name of a song you love and three things you like about it (the beat, the mood, the words). These are ideas you can learn from without copying the song.
You can now name ways AI is used in music and explain the rules for using it fairly.

check.q: Which is one way AI is used in music?
check.why: AI suggests chords, cleans up recordings, helps with lyrics and can generate songs.

check.q: A song generator makes a whole track from your one-line prompt. Can you call it fully your work?
options: Yes, the prompt makes you the author
No; prompts alone are not enough, so make the main creative choices yourself
check.why: The U.S. Copyright Office said typing prompts alone is not enough to make you the author.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Making your first beat in a free online studio
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Open a free online studio and make a 4-bar beat with drums and one other sound.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free online studio such as BandLab, with a parent's or guardian's OK, you will make a 4-bar beat with drums and one other sound at a tempo that fits the mood, playing back without gaps.
BandLab is a free music app and website with an online studio for making music. You can use it in a web browser at bandlab.com or in its app from the official app store. You need an account, so involve a parent or guardian when you sign up.
Music is counted in beats and bars. Most pop and hip-hop songs have 4 beats in a bar. A loop is a short piece of music that repeats. Many beats start with a drum loop, then add bass, then one more sound like keys or guitar.
Menus change over time, so look for these actions: start a new project, add a track, pick an instrument or browse loops, drag a loop onto the track, and press play. Change the tempo (speed) to fit the mood: slower for chill, faster for hype.
Step by step:
- With a parent or guardian, sign up for BandLab or another free online studio.
- Start a new project.
- Add a drum track, using a loop or by tapping in a simple pattern.
- Add a bass or keys track that fits the drums.
- Set the tempo, make it 4 bars long, and press play.
Words to know:
- Beat: the steady pulse of music; also a short instrumental track.
- Bar: a group of beats, usually 4.
- Loop: a short piece of music that repeats.
- Tempo: how fast the music goes, counted in beats per minute (BPM).
Official sources:
- BandLab Terms of Use (age and parent permission)
Try it now: Make a 4-bar beat with drums and one other sound. Try two different tempos and keep the one that fits the mood you want.
You can now open a free online studio and build a short beat from tracks and loops.

check.q: What is a bar in music?
options: A group of beats, usually 4 in pop and hip-hop
check.why: Music is counted in beats and bars, and most pop and hip-hop songs have 4 beats in a bar.

check.q: Your beat should feel hype, but it sounds sleepy. What do you change?
check.why: Tempo is the speed: faster for hype, slower for chill.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Brainstorming lyrics with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to brainstorm a theme and rhymes, then write lyrics in your own words.
This lesson builds toward: Given a theme from your own life, you will use AI to brainstorm images and rhymes, then write four lines of lyrics in your own words, so the lines fit the beat when said out loud.
Start with a theme from your life: first day at a new school, a summer job, a friend moving away, making the team. Real feelings make better songs than general ones.
Ask AI for ideas, not a finished song: "Give me 10 images and phrases about the last day of summer before high school" or "Give me rhyming words for 'late' and 'wait'." Then pick what you like and write the lines yourself.
Count syllables so the words fit the beat. Read your lines out loud over the beat. If a line feels crowded, cut words. Your lyrics should sound like you.
Step by step:
- Choose a theme from your own life.
- Ask AI for images, phrases or rhymes, not a full song.
- Write four lines in your own words.
- Say them out loud over your beat.
- Cut or change words until they fit.
Words to know:
- Lyrics: the words of a song.
- Theme: what a song is about.
- Syllable: one beat of sound in a word; "mu-sic" has two.
Try it now: Pick a theme, ask an AI assistant for 10 images or phrases about it, and write four lines of lyrics in your own words that fit your beat.
You can now brainstorm with AI and write original lyrics that fit a beat.

check.q: What should you ask AI for when writing lyrics?
options: Ideas such as images, phrases or rhymes
check.why: AI gives ideas; you write the lines yourself so they sound like you.

check.q: One line feels crowded when you say it over the beat. What do you do?
options: Cut or change words until it fits
check.why: Counting syllables and cutting words helps lines fit the beat.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Building, protecting and sharing your track

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building a song structure
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Arrange your track into an intro, verse and chorus.
This lesson builds toward: Given your beat and lyrics, you will arrange the track into an intro, verse and chorus, about 60 seconds long, with each part sounding a little different.
Most songs are built from parts. The intro opens the song. The verse tells the story and changes words each time. The chorus is the catchy part that repeats. A short song might go: intro, verse, chorus.
Make each part feel a little different. For example, the intro has only keys, the verse adds drums, and the chorus adds bass and a melody. Copy and paste sections in the studio to build the song along the timeline.
You can ask AI: "I have a 4-bar beat at 90 BPM. How could I arrange a 60-second song with an intro, verse and chorus?" Then try its ideas and trust your ears.
Step by step:
- Plan the order: intro, verse, chorus.
- Copy your beat to make each section.
- Take sounds out or add sounds so each part feels different.
- Put your lyrics on the verse and chorus.
- Play the whole thing and adjust.
Words to know:
- Intro: the opening of a song.
- Verse: the part that tells the story; words change each time.
- Chorus: the catchy part that repeats.
- Arrangement: how the parts of a song are ordered and layered.
Try it now: Arrange your beat into an intro, verse and chorus of about 60 seconds. Add your four lines of lyrics as text notes or record them if you want.
You can now arrange a track into clear song parts that each feel different.

check.q: What does the intro of a song do?
check.why: The intro opens the song before the verse and chorus.

check.q: Your intro, verse and chorus all sound the same. What do you do?
options: Take sounds out or add sounds so each part feels different
check.why: Changing which sounds play in each part makes the structure clear.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Copyright, samples and voices
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Decide whether a sound or voice is OK to use in your track.
This lesson builds toward: For every sound and voice in your track, you will decide whether each sound or voice is OK to use, and remove anything you cannot show is allowed, with no copied songs, unlicensed samples or AI copies of real voices.
Copyright protects original works like songs and recordings. According to the U.S. Copyright Office, a work is protected as soon as it is created and fixed in a form people can hear or see, and registration is generally voluntary. So most songs you hear are protected, and the song you make is yours.
Using a piece of someone else's recording is called sampling. Do not sample songs unless you have permission or the sound comes from a library that says you may use it, such as the loops in your studio. Read the tool's rules.
Voices are personal. Do not make or use an AI copy of a real person's voice, whether a star, a teacher or a classmate, without their clear permission. If you are not sure something is OK, leave it out or ask a teacher or parent.
Step by step:
- Ask: did I make this sound, or does the tool say I may use it?
- If it comes from someone else's song, leave it out unless you have permission.
- Never use an AI copy of a real person's voice without permission.
- When unsure, leave it out or ask a trusted adult.
Words to know:
- Copyright: the legal right of a creator to control copies of their work.
- Sample: a piece of someone else's recording used in a new track.
- Voice clone: an AI copy of a real person's voice.
Official sources:
- U.S. Copyright Office: Copyright basics FAQ
- U.S. Copyright Office: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
Try it now: List every sound in your track and where it came from: made by you, a studio loop, or something else. Remove anything you cannot say is OK to use.
You can now check every sound and voice in your track and keep only what you are allowed to use.

options: Using a piece of someone else's recording in a new track
check.why: Sampling means using part of someone else's recording.

check.q: You found a cool sound online but cannot tell who made it or if you may use it. What do you do?
options: Use it; no one will notice
Speed it up so it sounds different
Leave it out or ask a trusted adult
check.why: If you cannot say a sound is OK to use, leave it out or ask.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Mixing, exporting and sharing safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Balance your track, export it, and share it with honest credits.
This lesson builds toward: When the track is finished, you will balance the mix, export the track and write an honest credit note, sharing only where your family agrees and keeping personal details private.
Mixing means setting how loud each track is so nothing drowns out the rest. Turn down anything too loud and listen on both headphones and a phone speaker.
Then export or save the track as an audio file using the studio's export or download option. Write a short credit note: your name or artist name, the title, and how you used AI, for example "AI helped brainstorm lyric ideas; all music and lyrics written and arranged by me."
Share safely: post only where your family agrees, keep your full name, school and location private if you post publicly, and think before turning comments on. If your track is for school, follow your teacher's rules about AI.
Step by step:
- Balance the volume of each track.
- Listen on headphones and a phone speaker.
- Export or save the track as an audio file.
- Write a credit note that says how you used AI.
- Share only where your family agrees, keeping personal details private.
Words to know:
- Mixing: balancing the volume of each track.
- Export: save your project as a file others can play.
- Credit note: a short note that says who made what.
Try it now: Final task: finish your 60-second original track with a beat, intro, verse and chorus and your own lyrics. Check every sound is OK to use, export it, and write a credit note that says how you used AI.
You can now make, mix, export and share an original track fairly and safely, with honest credits.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Beat No drums, or only one sound. A beat with drums and at least one other sound at a tempo that fits the mood. The learner can explain why they chose that tempo. Song structure No clear intro, verse or chorus. About 60 seconds with an intro, verse and chorus that sound a little different. The chorus clearly stands out, for example with added bass or melody. Own lyrics Lyrics are missing or copied from AI. At least four lines in the learner's own words that fit the beat. Lyrics use a real theme from the learner's life and show AI ideas that were changed. Original and allowed Uses a copied song, an unlicensed sample or an AI copy of a real voice. Every sound is made by the learner or allowed by the studio, and no real voice is copied. Includes a list of each sound and where it came from. Export and credit Not exported, or no credit note. Exported as an audio file with a credit note that says how AI was used. The mix was checked on headphones and a phone speaker and adjusted. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Setting how loud each track is so nothing drowns out the rest
check.why: Mixing balances the volume of each track.

check.q: You want to post your track publicly. What do you keep private?
options: Your full name, school and location
check.why: Share safely by keeping personal details private and posting only where your family agrees.
